findings.title: AI-enabled schemes are not considered

findings.why: These schemes defeat controls that rely on recognising a person or a document.
findings.position: The answers about AI-enabled fraud cannot both be right as given: one says AI-enabled schemes are assessed for every relevant process, the other that, for high-risk processes, the assessment does not ask how AI could be used against them.

reported.question: Does it cover AI-enabled fraud, such as deepfake voice or video instructions, synthetic identities and AI-generated documents?
reported.answer: AI-enabled schemes, including deepfake instructions, synthetic identities and generated documents, are assessed for every relevant process.

furtherWeaknesses: Controls tested against AI fakes is not in place. It is a further defence against the same scenario and does not change the answer given for AI-enabled fraud covered.
Own AI tools in scope is partly in place. It is a further defence against the same scenario and does not change the answer given for AI-enabled fraud covered.

findings.title: Risks above tolerance are left without action
findings.how: Assessment results do not change controls, audit work or training.
findings.position: A response is reported as decided for every risk above tolerance, while rating each risk for likelihood and harm is reported as not in place. Risks above tolerance can be identified without ratings, but the answers do not say how this is done.

reported.question: Where a risk is above tolerance, is a response decided, such as adding controls, changing the process, insuring or accepting the risk?
reported.answer: The effect of each response is checked, and the response is revisited if the risk does not come down.

questions: Without likelihood and harm ratings, how does management identify which fraud risks are above tolerance and need a decided response?
methodRisks: Effort and audit work not directed at the highest fraud risks

findings.title: Invoices are paid for goods or services not received or not agreed
findings.how: Overbilling, fictitious deliveries or inflated rates are paid.
findings.why: Invoices paid without checking approval and receipt are how overbilling and fictitious deliveries get paid.
findings.position: Every invoice is reported as checked against an approved order and a confirmation of receipt before payment, while recording receipt of goods before payment is reported as partly in place. The check may rely on another confirmation where receipt is not recorded; the answers do not say which. Every invoice, including for services, is reported as checked against a confirmation of receipt before payment, while confirmation of delivery by the person who received the service is reported as not in place. Someone else may confirm delivery; the answers do not say who.

reported.question: Before an invoice is paid, is it checked against what was approved, such as an order, quote or contract, and against confirmation that the goods or services were received?
reported.answer: Every invoice is checked against an approved order, quote or contract and against confirmation of receipt before payment, and differences are resolved first.

furtherWeaknesses: Approved order before commitment is partly in place. It is a further defence against the same scenario and does not change the answer given for three-way match.

pathways.title: Invoices are paid for goods that were never delivered or services never performed

structure.title: Invoices are paid for goods that were never delivered or services never performed
structure.actor: A supplier inflating its billing, sometimes with the help of an employee who approves the invoices.
structure.opportunity: Invoices are paid on approval, without a consistent check that what is invoiced was ordered and received.
structure.entryPoint: An invoice for a delivery, a service or a rate that differs from what was agreed or received.
structure.mechanism: The invoice is approved by someone who did not receive the goods or confirm the service, and it is paid in the normal run.
structure.controlRelied: Receipt is not recorded before payment for every invoice, and service delivery is not confirmed by the person who received it.
structure.concealment: The invoice carries an approval, so it looks properly processed; overbilling is hidden among ordinary invoices.
structure.consequence: Continuing overpayment, which grows where an employee shares in it, and spend that cannot be reconciled to what the organisation actually received.
warningIndicators: Invoices without a matching receipt or delivery note
Service invoices approved by people far from the work
One approver for a supplier's invoices over a long period
structure.containment: Hold payment on the suspect invoices, reconcile them to orders and receipts, and preserve the approval trail.
structure.longTerm: Every invoice is matched to an approved order and a recorded receipt or confirmed service before payment.

pathways.title: A deepfake instruction, synthetic identity or generated document defeats a control that relies on recognition

structure.title: A deepfake instruction, synthetic identity or generated document defeats a control that relies on recognition
structure.actor: An outsider using AI tools to imitate a known person, create a synthetic identity or generate a convincing document.
structure.opportunity: Several controls rely on recognising a voice, a face, a signature or a document, and AI can now imitate each of them cheaply.
structure.entryPoint: An instruction, application or document presented through the organisation's ordinary channels.
structure.mechanism: The control does what it was designed to do, but the thing it recognises is fake, so a payment, account or approval is granted on false grounds.
structure.controlRelied: The fraud risk assessment has not asked, for each high-risk process, how AI could be used against the controls in it, so the controls have not been tested or redesigned for this.
structure.concealment: The control appears to have operated correctly, so the failure is not visible in its records.
structure.consequence: Losses through controls that management believes are effective, and a fraud risk assessment that understates exposure in exactly the processes that matter.
warningIndicators: Requests that rely only on recognising a person or document
Documents with flawless formatting from new counterparties
Video or voice contact that avoids interaction
Identity details that fit together too neatly
structure.containment: Confirm the instruction or document with its source through a separate known channel, and suspend reliance on recognition-only checks in the process concerned.
structure.longTerm: The fraud risk assessment asks, for each high-risk process, how AI could be used against its controls, and controls that rely on recognition are tested and redesigned.

pathways.title: Split orders and duplicate invoices pass because nobody looks across the payments

structure.title: Split orders and duplicate invoices pass because nobody looks across the payments
structure.actor: A buyer or finance clerk acting alone, or a supplier who deliberately invoices twice.
structure.opportunity: Each order and each invoice is checked on its own, so a pattern that only shows across many transactions is never seen.
structure.entryPoint: A purchase split into several orders that each fall under the approval limit, or an invoice resubmitted with a changed number or date.
structure.mechanism: Each order is approved within its limit and each invoice passes its own checks, so a purchase that should have gone to tender, or an invoice already paid, is processed in the ordinary way.
structure.controlRelied: No one independent of processing reviews the supplier payments as a population, for splitting, duplicates, unfamiliar suppliers or changed bank details.
structure.concealment: Every individual transaction is within policy; only the pattern is wrong, and the pattern is in data that nobody examines.
structure.consequence: Overpayment, purchases that bypass competitive tender, and a continuing loss that grows with each payment run until a supplier, an auditor or a whistle-blower raises it.
warningIndicators: Several orders to one supplier just below an approval limit
Invoices with the same amount and supplier close together
A supplier paid more often than its contract suggests
Orders raised and received by the same person
structure.containment: Stop further payments on the suspect orders or invoices, recover any duplicate payment from the supplier, and preserve the order, approval and payment records.
structure.longTerm: A senior manager who does not process payments reviews each month's supplier payments for splitting, duplicates, unfamiliar suppliers and changed bank details, and follows up each query.

priorities.title: Settle the answers about AI-enabled schemes
priorities.why: Nothing should be built on an answer that may be wrong.
priorities.establish: The answers about AI-enabled fraud cannot both be right as given: one says AI-enabled schemes are assessed for every relevant process, the other that, for high-risk processes, the assessment does not ask how AI could be used against them.
priorities.measure: The answers agree with each other and with how the process runs, and the corrected answer is recorded.

priorities.title: Answer the five questions the answers leave open
priorities.why: Each answer decides whether a control reported in place can be relied on.
priorities.establish: Without likelihood and harm ratings, how does management identify which fraud risks are above tolerance and need a decided response? For deliveries where receipt is not recorded before the invoice is paid, what confirmation of receipt does the invoice check rely on, and who gives it? For service invoices, who confirms that the service was delivered before payment, and is that confirmation recorded? Without a maintained list of high-risk roles, how does management confirm that the block leave requirement reaches every sensitive role? What is each stock count compared with to identify losses, given that stock is not formally recorded? When suspected fraud is investigated, does a line manager ever investigate a matter in the area they manage, and if so, how is independence achieved?
priorities.practicalOwner: Fraud risk lead, Finance lead, HR and payroll lead and Investigations lead
priorities.measure: Each question has a written answer from the process owner, and the assessment is corrected where needed.

priorities.title: Senior review of supplier payments
priorities.establish: Each month a senior manager who does not process payments reviews the list of supplier payments for unfamiliar suppliers, unusual amounts and changed bank details, and follows up each query.
priorities.measure: The review of supplier payments ran monthly throughout the period, and every exception it raised has a recorded answer.

priorities.title: Recipients checked for links
priorities.establish: Before any donation or sponsorship is committed, the recipient is checked for links to public officials, customers' decision-makers and employees, and any link found is disclosed and approved.
priorities.measure: Every donation or sponsorship in the period has a donation approval file showing the link checks completed and approved before money was committed.

priorities.title: Hours approved by supervisor
priorities.establish: Hours and overtime are approved by the employee's supervisor, against the roster or attendance record, before they are paid.
priorities.measure: Every timesheet paid in the period was approved by the employee's supervisor, against the roster or attendance record, before payment.

priorities.title: Losses tracked and reported
priorities.establish: Losses of cash, stock and assets are tracked over time and by location, and reported to management each month with the actions taken.
priorities.measure: The review of losses of cash, stock and assets ran monthly throughout the period, and every exception it raised was reported to management with the action taken.

decisions.question: Have the answers that cannot both be right settled, and the questions the answers leave open answered, before the controls concerned are relied on.
decisions.why: 1 scenario has answers that cannot both be right and 5 scenarios raise questions that the answers do not settle.
decisions.when: Before the controls concerned are relied on or reported as in place.
decisions.delay: The organisation may rely on a control whose operation the answers do not establish.

options.label: Process owners confirm and correct
options.description: Each process owner establishes how the process actually runs, records the answer and corrects the assessment where it was wrong.
options.effort: Low: a few hours per process owner.
options.benefit: Fast, and keeps ownership with the people who run the processes.
options.tradeOff: Relies on the same people whose answers are in question.

options.label: Internal walkthrough by someone independent of the process
options.description: A manager from another area, or internal audit where it exists, walks through each process with its owner and records what was seen.
options.effort: Moderate: a day or two per process.
options.benefit: An answer that does not rest only on the owner's view.
options.tradeOff: Takes longer and draws on people outside the process.

options.label: Independent validation through MK Advisory
options.description: MK examines the records and walks through the processes concerned, as a separately scoped engagement.
options.benefit: An independent view of whether the controls operate, which the automated assessment cannot give.
options.tradeOff: Cost and time; worthwhile where the answers concern controls the organisation relies on heavily.

options.recommended: Process owners confirm and correct, with an independent walkthrough for any answer that is still disputed.
options.rationale: The answers concern how the organisation's own processes run, which its owners can establish quickly; an independent view is needed only where that does not settle the question.

decisions.question: Name one accountable executive for each area with open or unresolved scenarios: fraud risk assessment (1), ethics (1), procurement (1), people (1) and assets (1).
decisions.why: Each scenario needs one person with authority over the process, the system and the people involved.
decisions.delay: Open scenarios have no owner, and the controls that stop them stay unassigned.

options.label: One accountable executive per area
options.description: Each area with open scenarios has one executive accountable for its controls, as the method suggests.
options.effort: Low to decide; ongoing for each executive.
options.benefit: Clear ownership that matches how the organisation is run.
options.tradeOff: Requirements that span areas, such as how changes to payment details are verified, need coordination across owners.

options.label: One executive for the whole programme
options.description: A single executive owns every open scenario and directs area leads.
options.benefit: One point of accountability and a consistent approach.
options.tradeOff: Area executives may treat the work as someone else's.

options.label: Area owners with a programme coordinator
options.description: Area executives own their scenarios, and the fraud risk lead coordinates requirements that span areas and reports progress.
options.benefit: Ownership stays in the areas while cross-area requirements are handled once.
options.tradeOff: Needs a coordinator with enough standing to hold owners to account.

options.recommended: Area owners with a programme coordinator.
options.rationale: The open scenarios sit in the operating areas, so ownership belongs there; several of the requirements span areas and are best designed once.

decisions.question: Decide the order in which the open scenarios are addressed, using explicit factors.
decisions.why: MK has not approved a method for rating fraud risks, so this report does not rank them, and neither its order nor the method's tiers is a ranking.
decisions.delay: Effort is spread across every scenario at once, or follows the order of this report, which is not a ranking.

options.label: Explicit factors, settled facts first
options.description: Answers to settle come first; then each open scenario is weighed on how far its control is reported in place, whether money, pay, cash or stock can leave without it, how much of the activity exists, and what management already knows of incidents.
options.benefit: A defensible order that management can explain to the oversight body.
options.tradeOff: Depends on information management must supply, such as volumes and known incidents.

options.label: Area by area
options.description: One area is completed before the next begins.
options.tradeOff: Requirements that span areas are designed several times, and exposure in later areas waits.

options.label: Cross-area requirements first
options.description: Requirements that span areas, such as verifying changes to payment details, are designed once and applied everywhere, before area-specific controls.
options.benefit: One design closes several scenarios at once.
options.tradeOff: Area-specific exposures wait until the shared designs are complete.

options.recommended: Explicit factors, settled facts first, applying cross-area requirements once where they arise.
options.rationale: An order of work should rest on facts management can state and defend to its oversight body, and designing shared requirements once avoids building the same control several times.

decisions.question: Have the board receive the status of the open and unresolved scenarios at each of its meetings until each is closed, deferred with a reason or accepted.
decisions.why: Regular reporting keeps the scenarios visible to the people who can remove blockers.
decisions.when: From the first meeting after this report.
decisions.delay: Progress is not visible until the next assessment.

options.label: At each meeting of the oversight body
options.description: A one-page status per open scenario at each meeting until it is closed, deferred with a reason or accepted.
options.benefit: Keeps the scenarios visible to the people who can remove blockers.
options.tradeOff: Adds to the oversight body's agenda.

options.label: Quarterly summary
options.benefit: Less frequent demand on the oversight body.
options.tradeOff: Blockers may wait a quarter before they are seen.

options.label: Exceptions only
options.description: Only scenarios that are late or blocked are reported.
options.tradeOff: The oversight body does not see progress, and a scenario can drift without being reported as an exception.

options.recommended: At each meeting of the oversight body, until each open scenario is closed, deferred with a reason or accepted.
options.rationale: Regular reporting is what keeps a programme moving once the first controls are in place.

items.deliverable: A written answer, added to the assessment record.

items.text: Answer the question the answers leave open for the scenario where an insider in a high-risk role works unchecked: without a maintained list of high-risk roles, how does management confirm that the block leave requirement reaches every sensitive role?
items.deliverable: A written answer, added to the assessment record.

items.text: Answer the question the answers leave open for the scenario where stock is stolen and hidden in the counts: what is each stock count compared with to identify losses, given that stock is not formally recorded?
items.deliverable: A written answer, added to the assessment record.

items.deliverable: A written answer, added to the assessment record.

legal.question: Criminal cases opened and followed
legal.text: Are criminal cases opened with the SAPS, or with the DPCI where section 34 of PRECCA applies, and is their progress followed up?

legal.question: Adequate procedures against bribery
legal.text: Section 34A of PRECCA makes a private-sector organisation or incorporated state-owned entity liable when a person associated with it pays a bribe, unless it had adequate procedures. Whether procedures are adequate is for a court to decide; this question records what is in place.

legal.question: Compromises reported as POPIA requires
legal.text: Is there a procedure to notify the Information Regulator, through its eServices portal, and the affected people of a security compromise as soon as reasonably possible after it is discovered, as section 22 of POPIA requires, with any delay justified and recorded?

selectionRules.themes: A theme is reported where the method supports a pattern: answers to settle together with weaker related practices (five or more), outstanding answers (five or more), areas fully in place set against areas mostly open (two or more of each), one area holding most open scenarios, or one of the method's cross-area objectives reported weaker in two or more areas. Up to five, in that order.
selectionRules.findings: Every scenario with answers to settle or a question to clarify, then one scenario from each theme in turn, choosing the one with more core controls reported absent, then more related practices reported weaker, then the method's order; up to 7. This is a selection rule, not a ranking: MK has not approved a prioritisation method.
selectionRules.pathways: Findings with an approved scenario structure, one per theme where possible; up to 3.
selectionRules.priorities: Settling answers comes first where there are any; then the controls that close the selected findings, controls to put in place before practices to strengthen, up to six in all.
selectionRules.blueprints: The controls among the priorities, up to five.

boundary: Every finding rests on the organisation's own answers. MK has not examined documents, interviewed staff or tested any control.
Records named are records management should maintain. MK has not reviewed them.
Independent evidence review and validation belong to MK Advisory, which is scoped and priced separately.
prohibited: Any score, maturity band or readiness level other than the labelled calculated test result
Any statement that a risk is high, critical, the most material or the highest priority
Any claim that a control was tested, verified, validated or confirmed by MK
Any incident, loss, Rand amount, supplier, system or person not in the Fact Pack
Any scenario, finding, control, decision option or owner not in the Fact Pack
